latin.411: ANNOTATIO III. De Transsubstantiatione ad pag. 36. in fine. Historia Transsubstantiationis Compendiolum complexa. §. I. Transsubstantiatio, si non quà nomen, certè quà rem, Consubstantiatione antiquior, rem absurdissimam, quam designat, apto satis, etsi serò admodum invento terminô, quà genericum saltem conceptum, expressam exhibet.
latin.412: Quemadmodum enim Transmutatio rei cujuscunque, transformatio vel exterioris, vel interioris formæ; sic Transsubstantiatio unius præcisè substantiæ in aliam (remanentibus sensibusque expositis prioris, seu transmutandæ, posterioris verò, seu in quam transitio fit, absorptis, nulli saltem sensui obviis Accidentibus) mutationem inaudito prorsus exemplo significat. Hujus Historiam, ob cognationem solùm cum Consubstantiatione, hoc locô, per compendium, tradituri, duas quasi Tractationis partes, constituemus, quarum Prior ORTUM Transsubstantiationis in caussis suis rimabitur: Posterior PROGRESSUM ejusdem in modis gradibusque conspicuum reddet.
latin.413: §. II. Inter Ortûs CAUSAS attendere quoque juvat Occasionalem, quam causam per accidens vocant. Hujusmodi alia Generalior, Specialior alia est. GENERALIOREM existimavero, Hyperbolicas, quin quandoque catachresticas Patrum, tam Græcorum, quàm Latinorum de Symbolis Eucharisticis, locutiones, quibus, nisi dextrè capiantur, incauti facile in errores abducuntur.
latin.414: Inter Græcorum Patrum dicta eminent ista CHRYSOSTOMI, Orientalium Patrum disertissimi: Conspicies ait, in sacra Eucharistia Dominum immolatum. Qui cum Patre sursum sedet in illo ipso temporis articulo, omnium manibus pertractatur. Ipsum vides, ipsum tangis, ipsum comedis. Neque enim Angelos neque Archangelos, sed ipsum horum omnium Dominum Tibi ostendo. In mysteriis sanguis ex Christi latere hauritur; hoc admirabili sanguine lingua cruentatur. Hom. 5. & 83. in Matth. Hom. 24. in 1. ad Corinth. Et rursus: Nos in unam secum massam reducit, nec se tantùm videri permittit, sed & tangi & manducari & dentes carni suæ infigi, adeo ut per cibum, quem nobis largitus est, in carnem suam convertamur. Hom. 45. in Johan.
latin.415: Ex Latinis, eloquentissimi AUGUSTINI verba hæcce adduxisse suffecerit Conc. 1. in Ps. 33. Ferebatur, inquit, Christus in manibus suis, quando, commendans ipsum corpus suum, ait: Hoc est Corpus meum; Ferebat enim illud corpus in manibus suis. Quibus omninò parallelum PROSPERI AQUITANICI de promis. & prædicat. part. 2. cap. 25. assertum: Dominus ait, suum corpus in sanctificato pane gestans manibus suis, dixit: Hoc est corpus meum. Hæc aliaque hujus farinæ Patrum hyperbolice satis enunciata, quibus una ex parte mysterii dignitatem amplificare atque extollere; Ex parte altera verò communicantes ab externorum symbolorum contemplatione ad res significatas tantò devotiùs meditandas convertere allaborarunt, nonnulli propriè nimis acceperunt, non attendentes, quibus iidem Patres hyperbolas suas haud rarò per restrictivas particulas QUASI, QUODAMMODO similesque, mitigarunt ac emolliverunt, annotante id ipsum perquam accuratè pontificio Autore eruditissimo Petro Picherello Opusc. Theol. à pag. 19. in fin. Si cui volupe est, plures Patrum hyperbolicas expressiones legere, haud frustra fuerit famigeratissimum Petrum de Marca Dissert. Posthuma de Euchar. Sacrament. p. 15. evolvere, quanquam in usum suum pontificium, i. e. abusum attractas, ideoque à B. Witakero vindicatas Tom. I. pag. 9.
latin.416: §. III. SPECIALIOR Transsubstantiationi ansa data fuit per varios Patrum, maximè Græcorum ἐμφατικωτέρας, pro genio linguæ, excogitatos terminos, quibus in specie mutationem istam, relativam partim, respectu scil. rei signatæ, partim mysticam, respectu communicantium fidelium, pani Eucharistico per & post consecrationem copulatam, designare soliti sunt, quales Autori nostro observati recitantur p. 450 & 480 necnon Salmasio in Tractat. de Transsubst. p. 1. μεταβολή scil. μεταμόρφωσις, μεταποίησις, μεταστοιχείωσις, μετατύπωσις, μεταρρυθμισμός, μετασκεύασις; singuli præterea propriis suis Autoribus tribuuntur à Joh. Jonstono de Communione c. 3. p. 113. Hi termini de morali & σχετικῇ mutatione à Patribus intellecti, substantialis mutationis opinionem aliis, procedente tempore, ingenerarunt.
latin.417: A Patribus interim nullam extra dictam Mutationem intellectam fuisse, probant, præter cætera, rationes hæ quatuor: (1) quòd expressè Patres docent, idque constantissimè, panes Eucharisticos post consecrationem manere semper idem, quòd ante fuerant. (2) quòd identidem panes post Consecrationem, Signa, Figuras, Symbola, Icones seu imagines, Typos, Antitypos, Similitudines, Metaphoras, Formas, Census, Species, appellant, sicque implicitè eorum versionem in corpus Christi inficiantur. Utramque rationem pluribus Patrum testimoniis confirmatam vide apud Jonston. citato tract. cap. 3. à pag. 82. ad 100. (3) quòd iisdem terminis utuntur Patres, quando fidelium cum Christo Unionem, per Sacræ Eucharistiæ usum debitum, describunt, probante ibidem eodem Jonstono cap. 5. à pag. 216. ad 225. (4) quòd adhuc terminos eosdem adhibent de aliis rebus variis locuti, quibus Conversionem Substantialem adscripsisse eos, nemini in mentem venerit. Pertinent huc verba Joh. Dunelmensis Histor. Transsubst. Papalis: Quid quod ipsi, inquit, Patres has easdem μεταβολῆς μεταποιήσεως & μεταστοιχείωσεως voces usurpant, cùm de Rebus aliis loquuntur, quæ substantiam suam, minimè vel amittunt vel mutant?

pass_a.411: ANNOTATIO III. On Transsubstantiation (to p. 36 at the end). A little Compendium embracing the History of Transsubstantiation. §. I. Transsubstantiation, if not as name, certainly as thing, is older than Consubstantiation; it exhibits the most absurd thing it designates, expressed by a term apt enough though invented quite late, at least as to the generic concept.
pass_a.412: For just as Transmutation of any thing whatever is a transformation of either exterior or interior form, so Transsubstantiation of precisely one substance into another (the accidents of the former, exposed to the senses, remaining, but those of the latter, into which the passage is made, absorbed and at least not obvious to any sense) signifies a mutation by an utterly unheard-of example. About to hand down its History here in a compendium, only because of kinship with Consubstantiation, we shall set two parts of the Tractation as it were: the Prior will probe the ORTUS of Transsubstantiation in its causes; the Posterior will make conspicuous its PROGRESSUS in modes and degrees.
pass_a.413: §. II. Among the CAUSES of the Ortus it also helps to attend to the Occasional, which they call a cause by accident. Of this sort one is More General, another More Special. I shall judge the MORE GENERAL to be the Hyperbolic, nay sometimes catachrestic, locutions of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, about the Eucharistic Symbols, by which, unless they are taken skillfully, the unwary are easily led off into errors.
pass_a.414: Among the sayings of the Greek Fathers these of CHRYSOSTOM, most eloquent of the Eastern Fathers, stand out: You will behold, he says, in the sacred Eucharist the Lord immolated. He who sits above with the Father is at that very instant of time handled by the hands of all. You see Him, you touch Him, you eat Him. For I show you neither Angels nor Archangels, but the Lord Himself of them all. In the mysteries blood is drawn from Christ’s side; with this admirable blood the tongue is stained. Hom. 5 & 83 on Matt.; Hom. 24 on 1 Cor. And again: He reduces us into one mass with Himself, and does not permit Himself only to be seen, but also to be touched and eaten and teeth to be fixed in His flesh, so that through the food He has bestowed we are converted into His flesh. Hom. 45 on John.
pass_a.415: From the Latins it will have sufficed to have adduced these words of most eloquent AUGUSTINE, Serm. 1 on Ps. 33: Christ was being carried in His own hands, he says, when, commending His very body, He said: This is My Body; for He was bearing that body in His hands. Wholly parallel is the assertion of PROSPER OF AQUITAINE, De promiss. & prædicat. part 2 ch. 25: The Lord said, bearing His body in the sanctified bread with His hands: This is My body. These and other sayings of that flour, hyperbolically enough uttered by the Fathers — by which on one side they labored to amplify the mystery’s dignity, on the other to turn communicants from contemplating the outward symbols toward meditating the things signified more devoutly — some took too properly, not attending that the same Fathers not rarely softened their hyperboles by restrictive particles QUASI, QUODAMMODO and the like, as the most learned pontifical Author Peter Picherellus notes most accurately (Opusc. Theol. from p. 19 to the end). If anyone delights to read more hyperbolic expressions of the Fathers, it will not be in vain to unroll the celebrated Peter de Marca’s posthumous Dissertation on the Eucharistic Sacrament p. 15 — though drawn into pontifical use, i.e. abuse, and therefore vindicated by Blessed Whitaker, Tom. I p. 9.
pass_a.416: §. III. A MORE SPECIAL handle was given to Transsubstantiation by various terms more emphatic, devised by the Fathers (especially the Greeks) according to the genius of the language, by which they were wont to designate specifically that mutation — partly relative with respect to the thing signified, partly mystic with respect to the communicating faithful — coupled to the Eucharistic bread through and after consecration; such as are recited as observed by our Author at pp. 450 & 480, and also by Salmasius in the Tractate on Transsubstantiation p. 1: namely μεταβολή, μεταμόρφωσις, μεταποίησις, μεταστοιχείωσις, μετατύπωσις, μεταρρυθμισμός, μετασκεύασις; and each is further assigned to its own Authors by John Johnston, De Communione ch. 3 p. 113. These terms, understood by the Fathers of a moral and σχετική mutation, in time generated in others the opinion of a substantial mutation.
pass_a.417: That meanwhile no Mutation beyond the said one was understood by the Fathers is proved, among the rest, by these four reasons: (1) that the Fathers expressly teach, and that most constantly, that the Eucharistic breads after consecration always remain the same that they were before. (2) that they repeatedly call the breads after Consecration Signs, Figures, Symbols, Icons or images, Types, Antitypes, Likenesses, Metaphors, Forms, Censuses, Species, and so implicitly deny their conversion into Christ’s body. See both reasons confirmed by many Father-testimonies in Johnston’s cited tract ch. 3 from p. 82 to 100. (3) that the Fathers use the same terms when they describe the Union of the faithful with Christ through due use of the Sacred Eucharist, as the same Johnston proves there ch. 5 from p. 216 to 225. (4) that they still apply the same terms when speaking of various other things to which no one would dream they ascribed a Substantial Conversion. Here belong the words of John of Durham’s History of Papal Transsubstantiation: What of it that the Fathers themselves, he says, usurp these same voices of μεταβολή, μεταποίησις and μεταστοιχείωσις when they speak of other Things that by no means either lose or change their substance?

411: Annotatio III opens on Transsubstantiation (to p. 36 end): a short History-compendium.
§.I: as rem (if not yet as name) it is older than Consubstantiation; the rem it names is most absurd; the term itself came late but fits the generic concept.
412: Transmutation reshapes form; Transsubstantiation turns one substance into another while sense-exposed accidents of the former remain and those of the latter are absorbed — a mutation without precedent.
Plan: ORTUS (causes) then PROGRESSUS (modes and degrees), treated here only for kinship with Consubstantiation.
413: §.II Ortus causes: also the Occasional (cause by accident).
GENERALIOR: hyperbolic — sometimes even catachrestic — Father-speech on Eucharistic symbols; mishandled, it leads the unwary into error.
414: Chrysostom (Eastern Fathers’ most eloquent): in the Eucharist you behold the immolated Lord — seated with the Father yet handled, seen, touched, eaten; blood from His side stains the tongue (Hom. Matt. / 1 Cor.).
Again: He knits us into one mass with Himself; teeth are fixed in His flesh so that by the food given we are turned into His flesh (Hom. 45 on John).
415: Augustine (Serm. 1 on Ps. 33): Christ was carried in His own hands when He said ‘This is My Body’; Prosper parallels Him bearing His body in the sanctified bread.
Such hyperboles aimed to exalt the mystery and turn communicants from outward symbols to the things signified — yet some took them too properly, missing QUASI / QUODAMMODO softenings (Picherellus).
More samples: de Marca’s posthumous Eucharist dissertation (pontifical abuse) — vindicated by Whitaker.
416: §.III SPECIALIOR handle: Greek emphatic change-terms (metabole, metamorphosis, metapoiesis, metastoicheiosis, metatyposis, metarrhythmismos, metaskeuasis) for a mutation relative to the thing signified and mystic for communicants — cited via our Author, Salmasius, Johnston.
Fathers meant moral and schetic (relative) change; later readers bred a substantial-mutation opinion from those words.
417: Four proofs Fathers meant no mutation beyond that: (1) consecrated breads remain what they were; (2) they are still called signs/figures/symbols/types — so conversion into Christ’s body is implicitly denied (Johnston).
(3) Same terms describe the faithful’s union with Christ by due Eucharist use; (4) same terms on other things no one takes as substantial conversion — Dunelm on that metabole vocabulary.
Stop before §.IV vera causa (idolatry and tyranny of Papism).
